definition: Morass means a wet, swampy bog — or, far more often in reading, a confusing, entangled situation that swallows time and effort.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word morass. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know morass should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: What began as a simple porch addition sank into a morass of permit forms, inspection backlogs, and conflicting instructions from the city office.
A muddle is a small mix-up — a double-booked meeting — that an afternoon can straighten out; a morass entangles you for weeks.
A nightmare goes beyond a morass: people reach for that word when a situation stops feeling merely tangled and starts feeling unbearable.

A tangle is a knotted, confused mess — cords, schedules, regulations twisted together — that you can set about unpicking strand by strand from the outside. A morass is a bog: you do not unpick it, you sink into it, and working harder only pulls you deeper.

A labyrinth is a bewildering maze with no clear way through — but you stay on your feet, wandering and lost. A morass takes you downward: it is the swamp that swallows time and effort. You wander into a labyrinth; you sink into a morass.

A snarl is a knot that jams one particular spot — a traffic snarl, a snarl in the supply chain. It is local, and traffic eventually crawls past it. A morass is the whole terrain gone soft: an entire undertaking swallowed by confusion, with no firm ground anywhere.

Preparing the food truck's first tax return meant wading through a morass of overlapping city, county, and state rules.
The rules overlap and pile on top of one another with no clear path through, which is exactly the entangling, bewildering mess that morass names — notice the owner is wading, not walking.
Formal; literal and figurative

Morass began as a literal word for a swamp and still works that way, but in modern reading it almost always means a situation that entangles and confuses — a morass of regulations, paperwork, or data.
Its cousins in this unit split the territory: a maelstrom batters you with churning violence, a quagmire holds you stuck, and a morass buries you in confusion.

The district bought new gradebook software with a promise: teachers would save an hour a week.
By October the rollout had thickened into a morass.
Every error ticket required a form, every form triggered a training, and every training produced new errors to report.
Teachers typed grades by hand at midnight while the help desk's backlog grew; the harder the IT office pushed, the further behind it fell.
In March the district quietly scrapped the system — six months of effort, sunk without a trace.
